'''''The Equidistribution of Lattice Shapes of Rings of Integers of Cubic, Quartic, and Quintic Number Fields: An Artist's Rendering''''' is a mathematics book by Piper Harron (also known as Piper H and Piper Harris), based on her [[Princeton University]] [[doctoral thesis]] of the same title. It has been described as "feminist",<ref name="molinari"/> "unique",<ref name="salerno"/> "honest",<ref name="salerno"/> "generous",<ref name="ording"/> and "refreshing".<ref name="lamb"/>

==Thesis and reception==
Harron was advised by [[Fields Medal]]ist [[Manjul Bhargava]], and her thesis deals with the properties of [[number fields]], specifically the shape of their [[rings of integers]].<ref name="salerno">{{cite journal |url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/MAAFocus/FOCUS_Feb_Mar_2019.pdf |pages=50–51 |title=Book review: Mathematics for the People |journal=[[MAA Focus]] |date=February–March 2019 |first=Adriana |last=Salerno |author-link=Adriana Salerno|volume=39 |number=1}}</ref><ref name="publisher">{{cite web <!-- Citation bot bypass-->|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783319765310 |title=The Equidistribution of Lattice Shapes of Rings of Integers of Cubic, Quartic, and Quintic Number Fields |website=Springer Nature Switzerland AG |access-date=June 18, 2021}}</ref> Harron and Bhargava showed that, viewed as a [[Lattice (group)|lattice]] in [[real vector space]], the ring of integers of a random number field does not have any special symmetries.<ref name="publisher"/><ref>{{cite conference |title=14th Meeting of the Canadian Number Theory Association |date=June 20–24, 2016 |chapter-url=https://prism.ucalgary.ca/bitstream/handle/1880/110341/cnta-program-small.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y |location=University of Calgary |first=Piper |last=Harron |chapter=Contributed Talks |page=26 |access-date=June 8, 2025 |archive-date=July 18, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210718012615/https://prism.ucalgary.ca/bitstream/handle/1880/110341/cnta-program-small.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y |url-status=live }}</ref> Rather than simply presenting the [[Mathematical proof|proof]], Harron intended for the thesis and book to explain both the mathematics and the process (and struggle) that was required to reach this result.<ref name="publisher"/>

The writing is accessible and informal, and the book features sections targeting three different audiences: laypeople, people with general mathematical knowledge, and experts in [[number theory]].<ref name="molinari">{{cite book |chapter=Re-imagining Doctoral Writings as Emergent Open Systems |title=Re-imagining doctoral writing |publisher=Colorado Press |first=Julia |last=Molinari |date=April 2021 |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351116844 |type=preprint}}</ref> Harron intentionally departs from the typical academic format as she is writing for a community of mathematicians who "do not feel that they are encouraged to be themselves".<ref name="molinari"/> Unusually for a mathematics thesis, Harron intersperses her rigorous analysis and proofs with cartoons, poetry, pop-culture references, and humorous diagrams.<ref name="salerno"/> Science writer Evelyn Lamb, in ''[[Scientific American]]'', expresses admiration for Harron for explaining the process behind the mathematics in a way that is accessible to non-mathematicians, especially "because as a woman of color, she could pay a higher price for doing it."<ref name="lamb">{{cite web |first=Evelyn |last=Lamb |publisher=[[Scientific American]] |title=Contrasts in Number Theory |date=December 28, 2015 |access-date=June 18, 2021 |url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/roots-of-unity/contrasts-in-number-theory/ |archive-date=July 11, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711190119/https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/roots-of-unity/contrasts-in-number-theory/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Mathematician Philip Ording calls her approach to communicating [[mathematical abstraction]]s "generous".<ref name="ording">{{cite conference |chapter=Creative Writing in Mathematics and Science |first=Philip |last=Ording |chapter-url=https://www.birs.ca/files/publications/proceedings/birs_2016_proceedings.pdf |title=Banff International Research Station Proceedings 2016 |year=2016 |page=7 |access-date=June 18, 2021 |archive-date=June 24, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624201114/https://www.birs.ca/files/publications/proceedings/birs_2016_proceedings.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

Her thesis [[Viral phenomenon|went viral]] in late 2015, especially within the mathematical community, in part because of the prologue which begins by stating that "respected research math is dominated by men of a certain attitude".<ref name="salerno"/><ref name="lamb"/> Harron had left academia for several years, later saying that she found the atmosphere oppressive and herself miserable and verging on failure.<ref name="kamanos">{{cite book |title=The Female Artist in Academia: Home and Away |first=Anastasia |last=Kamanos |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |year=2019 |isbn=9781793604118 |page=21 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mp27DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA21}}</ref> She returned determined that, even if she did not do math the "right way", she "could still contribute to the community".<ref name="kamanos"/> Her prologue states that the community lacks diversity and discourages diversity of thought.<ref name="lamb"/> "It is not my place to make the system comfortable with itself", she concludes.<ref name="lamb"/>

A concise proof was published in ''[[Compositio Mathematica]]'' in 2016.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bhargava|first1=Manjul|last2=Harron|first2=Piper|date=June 2016|title=The equidistribution of lattice shapes of rings of integers in cubic, quartic, and quintic number fields|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/compositio-mathematica/article/equidistribution-of-lattice-shapes-of-rings-of-integers-in-cubic-quartic-and-quintic-number-fields/77022FD0F7790FD83E19886C89893638|journal=[[Compositio Mathematica]]|volume=152|issue=6|pages=1111–1120|arxiv=1309.2025|doi=10.1112/S0010437X16007260|mr=3518306|zbl=1347.11074|s2cid=118043017|archive-date=June 25, 2021|access-date=June 18, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210625040931/https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/compositio-mathematica/article/equidistribution-of-lattice-shapes-of-rings-of-integers-in-cubic-quartic-and-quintic-number-fields/77022FD0F7790FD83E19886C89893638|url-status=live}}</ref>
